newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Dec 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - Dec 10.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Tuesday:
- Clothing catalogue companies are finding themselves shorter on inventory than they have been in at least three years.
- Many power companies are preoccupied with finding merger partners rather than adding to existing overcapacity by building power plants.
- The Homestake Mining Co offered $2.3 billion to acquire Santa Fe Pacific Gold.
- A Federal jury in Brooklyn awarded nearly $6 million to three women who sustained arm, wrist and hand injuries while using keyboards made by the Digital Equipment Corp.
- Stocks continued a recovery from Friday's early selloff.
- The Microsoft Network is expected to emerge from its face lift by looking to a broader audience, in part by emulating TV.
- German corporations are giving in to unions after vowing to cut sick pay.
- Monsanto said it would spin off its $3 billion chemicals business to shareholders.
- Mastercard is taking aim at American Express's customer base by introducing a new travel-oriented card.
- Four companies accused of fixing the price of citric acid have agreed to pay $94 million to settle a class action suit.
- Netscape Communications announced a marketing agreement under which five regional telephone operating companies will make Netscape Navigator their primary browser software for the Internet.
- A former AT&T executive who was part of one of the largest insider trading cases on record agreed to pay more than $813,000 to settle SEC charges.
- Ashland Inc said it would cut spending on its core refining business and focus more on its other businesses.

- Acromed has agreed to pay $112 million to settle claims by patients who said that the pain in their backs grew worse after surgeons inserted steel screws from the company that were meant to help them.
- Volkswagen expressed regret to General Motors for the "trouble and costs" caused by the dispute over VW's hiring of a top GM executive, who faces allegations on industrial espionage.
- Two closely-watched forecasters cheered Madison Avenue with predictions of higher advertising spending for 1997 and the rest of the decade.
